subject: English
source: National Curriculum Year 3 English (grammar, spelling and fable writing); Drive English folder held no KS2 material so content is original

lessons.title: Nouns and expanded noun phrases
objectives: Identify common and proper nouns
Build an expanded noun phrase with adjectives and a prepositional phrase

keywords.def: a word that names a person, place, thing or idea
a word that describes a noun
a noun with the words that go with it, such as the old wooden boat
a word that shows position or time, such as under, beside, before

starter: Say bismillah. Write the four types of sentence you learnt in Year 2.
Add a capital letter and full stop: the baker sold warm bread
Give two adjectives to describe a lion.

teach.heading: Nouns name things
bullets: Common nouns: boy, mosque, apple, kindness
Proper nouns name one special person or place
Proper nouns begin with a capital letter: Layla, Makkah, Monday
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a quick game: name a noun for each thing you can see on screen. Sort their answers into common and proper nouns. Misconception: children capitalise every noun. Stress that only names of particular people, places, days and months need capitals.

teach.heading: Adjectives add detail
bullets: a tall tree, a rusty key, a gentle breeze
Choose precise adjectives, not just big or nice
teach.note: Show a plain sentence: 'The boy found a key.' Ask which adjectives could make us see it. Collect: rusty, tiny, golden. Ask why 'tiny golden key' creates a different picture from 'heavy iron key'. Push for precise vocabulary over common words like nice, good, big.

teach.heading: Expanded noun phrases
bullets: Add where: the old wooden boat on the river
teach.note: Build one phrase on the board in layers: boat, the boat, the old boat, the old wooden boat, the old wooden boat on the river. Explain that a noun phrase tells us more about a noun and can act as the subject of a sentence. Point out that 'on the river' is a prepositional phrase.

teach.heading: Using noun phrases in sentences
bullets: The small, brown dog with floppy ears barked.
Read both: which helps you picture the dog?
teach.note: Compare the two sentences. Model rereading for sense. Mention that two adjectives before a noun are separated by a comma, unless one of them is a number or colour that fits tightly with the noun. Do not overload; stretch pupils only.

teach.heading: Check and improve
bullets: Have I used a capital letter and full stop?
teach.note: Model improving one sentence from the class. Ask pupils to use mini-whiteboards to expand 'The cat sat.' Praise the use of a prepositional phrase to say where.

practice: Sort into common and proper: Madinah, river, Saturday, teacher, Omar
Expand the noun phrase: a bird (add two adjectives)
Expand again with where: the cave
independent: Write five sentences about a market. Each must have an expanded noun phrase with an adjective and a prepositional phrase.
Underline the noun phrases in your sentences.
Rewrite 'The man carried a bag' in three more detailed ways.
exit: Write an expanded noun phrase about a mosque garden.
Which word in 'the old wooden boat' is the noun?
lessons.homework: Write three sentences about your bedroom using expanded noun phrases.
lessons.send: SEND: give a word bank and picture prompts. EAL: label pictures with adjectives first. Stretch: add two adjectives with a comma and one prepositional phrase.

lessons.title: Verbs and tense: present perfect
objectives: Recognise simple past and present tense verbs
Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) correctly

keywords.def: a word that shows an action, state or event
shows when something happens
has/have + past participle, such as I have eaten
a verb that does not add -ed in the past

starter: Bismillah. Is this past or present: She walks to school?
Write the past tense of: jump, play, carry
Underline the verb: The children read quietly.

teach.heading: Verbs and tense
bullets: Verbs tell us what is happening
Present: I walk. Past: I walked.
teach.note: Ask pupils to act out verbs. Establish that every sentence needs a verb. Revise: add -ed for most past tense verbs, but remember spelling changes such as carry to carried.

teach.heading: Irregular past tense
teach.note: Say each verb and its past tense in a chant. Misconception: 'goed' and 'eated'. Explain that these verbs are irregular and have to be learnt, so we practise them often.

teach.heading: The present perfect
bullets: Pattern: have or has + past participle
teach.note: Explain that the present perfect links the past to now: 'I have finished' means the work is done now. Use a time line. Contrast with simple past: 'I finished my work yesterday.' The simple past names a finished time; the present perfect does not.

teach.heading: Past participles that change
bullets: Wrong: I have went. Right: I have gone.
teach.note: Choral practice. Write 'I seen' and 'I have went' on the board as common errors in speech and ask pupils to correct them. Explain that Standard English uses the participle after have/has.

teach.heading: Choosing the tense
bullets: We have visited the park three times (present perfect)
teach.note: Give clue words: yesterday, last week mean simple past; already, just, so far suggest present perfect. Ask for oral sentences with each clue.

practice: Change to the past tense: I go, we see, they write
Fill the gap: She has ___ (eat) her dinner.
Correct: I have went to the shop.
independent: Complete ten sentences using the correct form of the verb in brackets (e.g. He has ___ (take) the book).
Write five sentences of your own using has or have + a past participle.
Find and correct three errors: I seen a bird. She have wrote a card. We has gone home.
exit: Write the present perfect of the verb eat with 'she'.
Correct: I have saw the sea.
lessons.homework: Write four sentences about what you have done today, using have or has.
lessons.send: SEND: use a table with verb, past, participle. EAL: practise with gestures and flash cards. Stretch: explain in a sentence the difference between I ate and I have eaten.

lessons.title: Conjunctions: when, if, because, although
objectives: Join two clauses with a range of conjunctions
Write longer sentences that are punctuated correctly

keywords.def: a word that joins words or clauses
a group of words with a verb
a conjunction that gives a reason
a conjunction that shows a contrast

starter: Bismillah. Join with and or but: I like apples ___ I do not like pears.
Underline the verb: The rain fell heavily.
Write a sentence starting with First.

teach.heading: Joining words
bullets: I was tired, so I went to bed.
teach.note: Revise Year 2 conjunctions. Show a pair of short sentences and ask pupils to join them using so. Explain that joining sentences makes writing flow and shows how ideas connect.

teach.heading: Because: giving a reason
bullets: I took an umbrella because it was raining.
teach.note: Ask pupils to say sentences orally using 'because'. Remind them a sentence with 'because' needs two parts: the main idea and the reason. A reason alone is not a sentence: 'Because it was raining.'

teach.heading: When, while and if
bullets: when: I smile when I see my friends.
while: Dad cooked while I set the table.
if: If it is sunny, we will play outside.
teach.note: Link each conjunction to time or condition. Practise by turning real class routines into sentences. Note that conjunctions can come at the start: 'If it is sunny, we will play outside.' A comma follows the first part.

teach.heading: Although: a surprise
bullets: Although it was cold, we played outside.
Compare: It was cold, but we played outside.
teach.note: Explain that although tells us that the second idea is unexpected. Compare with but. Ask pupils to complete 'Although I was tired, ...' orally with a partner.

teach.heading: Check punctuation
teach.note: Model checking two sentences. Emphasise that the comma comes after the first part when the conjunction opens the sentence: 'Although it was late, we kept reading.'

practice: Choose the best conjunction: I stayed inside ___ it was raining. (because/but)
Complete: Although I was hungry, ...
Join: Hana ran. She wanted to catch the bus. (because)
independent: Join ten pairs of sentences using a suitable conjunction.
Write sentences using when, if, because and although about a trip to the park.
Rewrite one sentence so that it begins with the conjunction.
exit: Write a sentence using because.
Write a sentence starting with Although.
lessons.homework: Write five sentences about your weekend, each with a different conjunction.
lessons.send: SEND: give sentence halves to match. EAL: provide a conjunction bank with example sentences. Stretch: write a sentence with two conjunctions.

lessons.title: Adverbs and prepositions of time, place and cause
objectives: Use adverbs to show how, when and why
Use prepositions to show time and place

keywords.def: a word that tells us more about a verb, such as quickly or soon
a word that links a noun to another word, such as under, before
a word or phrase that tells when something happens, such as then or next
a word that shows a result

starter: Bismillah. Underline the adjective: the sleepy cat.
Write one noun phrase.
Write a sentence with the conjunction although.

teach.heading: What do adverbs do?
bullets: They tell us how, when or where
teach.note: Act out walking slowly, loudly and quietly. Ask which word tells us how the action is done. Misconception: not all adverbs end in -ly (soon, often).

teach.heading: Time adverbs for order
bullets: First, next, then, soon, later, finally
Then we shared it with our neighbours.
teach.note: Use time adverbs to sequence a short routine such as making wudu. Check each step reads clearly and ask pupils to say it out loud using three different time adverbs.

teach.heading: Cause adverbs
bullets: It was dark. Therefore, we switched on the light.
teach.note: Explain that therefore links a cause to its result, and that because of is followed by a noun phrase: 'We stayed in because of the rain.' Compare 'because it rained' with 'because of the rain'.

teach.heading: Prepositions of place and time
bullets: The cat hid under the table.
teach.note: Use a cup and a table on camera to demonstrate placing the cup under, beside, behind. Ask where it is. Show time prepositions: 'before prayer', 'after school', 'during lessons'.

teach.heading: Put it together
bullets: Soon, the cat crept through the fence.
After lunch, we played beside the river.
teach.note: Model joining adverbials to sentences. Ask pupils to improve a dull sentence 'The boy went home.' Collect improvements and reread.

practice: Choose an adverb: She spoke ___ . (quietly/quiet)
Circle the preposition: The ball rolled under the bench.
Add a time adverb: ___ , we packed our bags.
independent: Write six sentences about a morning routine using different time adverbs.
Write four sentences using prepositions of place to describe a picture.
Complete: It rained all day. Therefore, ...
exit: Write a sentence using because of.
Underline the adverb in: The bird sang sweetly.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph about a walk in the park using at least three adverbs and three prepositions.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards for adverbs and meanings. EAL: act out prepositions with objects. Stretch: write a paragraph using four different time adverbs without repeating any.

lessons.title: Prefixes: un-, dis-, mis-, re-, in-
objectives: Explain how prefixes change meaning
Spell words with prefixes correctly

keywords.def: letters added to the front of a word to change its meaning
the main word before a prefix or suffix is added
a word with the reverse meaning
a word that means the opposite of another word

starter: Bismillah. Spell: happy, kind, lock.
What is a noun? Give two examples.
Write the past tense of write and eat.

teach.heading: What is a prefix?
bullets: Added to the front of a root word
The spelling of the root stays the same
teach.note: Write 'happy' and add un-. Ask how the meaning changes. A prefix is a group of letters placed before a root word. Explain that we do not change the root word spelling.

teach.heading: un- and in-: not
teach.note: Both un- and in- often mean 'not'. Ask pupils to say sentences using unhappy, unkind and inactive. Stress that we cannot always swap them: 'inhappy' is not a word. Check with a dictionary.

teach.heading: dis- and mis-
bullets: dis- means not or opposite: disagree
teach.note: Explain that mis- shows something done wrongly. Show 'mis + spell = misspell' (two s) and 'dis + appear = disappear' (one p). 'dis + satisfied = dissatisfied' has two s's because satisfied begins with s.

teach.heading: re-: again
teach.note: Explain that re- means again or back. Ask where we use these words: rewrite our work, reheat food. We only learn common examples at this stage.

teach.heading: Use a prefix to build opposites
teach.note: Give pupils a word and a prefix. Ask them to say the new word aloud in a sentence. Close by checking spellings with sound buttons.

practice: Add a prefix: __happy, __agree, __spell
What does re- mean in rebuild?
Spell: disappear
independent: Make ten new words by adding un-, dis-, mis- or re- to root words (lock, like, behave, read, fair, obey, place, heat, honest, take).
Write a sentence for each of five of your new words.
Sort the words into two columns: not or opposite / again or wrongly.
exit: Add a prefix to the word 'lock' to mean 'open the lock'.
Spell the word that means 'to spell wrongly'.
lessons.homework: Find six words with un-, dis-, mis- or re- at home and write them in sentences.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a prefix bank and fewer root words. EAL: use pictures and gestures. Stretch: find words with the prefixes sub-, super- or anti- and explain their meanings.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Reading a fable: The Hare and the Tortoise
objectives: Describe the features of a fable
Retrieve and explain information from a short text

keywords.def: a short story with animal characters that teaches a lesson
the lesson a story teaches
a person or animal in a story
find information in a text

starter: Bismillah. Name one conjunction and use it in a sentence.
What does the prefix mis- mean?
Write an expanded noun phrase about a river.

teach.heading: What is a fable?
bullets: A short story with a lesson
A fable ends with a moral
Aesop is the best-known writer of fables
teach.note: Introduce fables as very old stories told to teach good behaviour. Ask pupils which stories with animals they know. Explain that the animals have one main quality, such as pride or kindness.

teach.heading: Read the fable
bullets: The hare boasts about his speed
They race to the oak tree
The hare naps; the tortoise keeps going
teach.note: Aesop's fable, retold: A hare laughed at a tortoise for being so slow. 'I could win any race with my eyes closed,' he boasted. 'Then let us race,' said the tortoise quietly. A fox marked the finish line at the old oak tree. 'Ready, steady, go!' The hare shot off and was soon far ahead. Looking back, he saw that the tortoise had hardly moved. 'I have plenty of time,' he yawned, and lay down under a tree for a nap. The tortoise plodded on, step by step, and never stopped. When the hare woke, the sun was low. He sprinted towards the oak tree, but the tortoise was already crossing the line. Moral: slow and steady wins the race. Read aloud with expression. Pause after the boast and ask pupils to predict what will happen.

teach.heading: Find the facts
bullets: Quote the text to prove it
teach.note: Model retrieval: find a sentence that answers 'Who marked the finish line?' Show how to scan for key words and underline the answer. Remind pupils to answer in a sentence.

teach.heading: Why did the tortoise win?
bullets: Boasting led to the hare's mistake
teach.note: Ask for answers starting 'The tortoise won because...'. Accept reasons from the text: the hare slept. Model a full sentence answer.

teach.heading: The moral
bullets: Slow and steady wins the race
The lesson is shown by what happens
teach.note: Ask the class to explain the moral in their own words. Link to Islam: the Prophet (peace be upon him) is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim to have said that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done regularly, even if small. Keep the link brief and respectful.

practice: Who marked the finish line?
Find and copy one word that shows the tortoise moved slowly.
What did the hare do instead of racing?
independent: Answer in full sentences: (a) What did the hare boast? (b) Where was the finish line? (c) Why was the hare late? (d) What is the moral?
Draw a story map with four boxes: boast, race, nap, finish.
List three features of a fable using the story as evidence.
exit: Write the moral of the fable.
Who is the main character who makes a mistake?
lessons.homework: Retell the fable to a family member and write the moral on a card.
lessons.send: SEND: read the story with a partner; give picture sequencing cards. EAL: pre-teach boasted, plodded, sprinted. Stretch: suggest another moral and defend it.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Characters and inference
objectives: Use evidence from the text to say what a character is like
Explain the meaning of words in context

keywords.def: work out something that the author does not say directly
words from the text that prove your idea
spoke proudly about what you can do
walked slowly and heavily

starter: Bismillah. What is a fable?
What is the moral of The Hare and the Tortoise?
Find the verb: The tortoise plodded on.

teach.heading: Inference
bullets: Authors do not tell us everything
We use clues to work it out
I think... because the text says...
teach.note: Show a picture of a child holding an umbrella and ask what the weather is. Explain that we use clues. Reading is detective work: we find evidence in the text to support our ideas.

teach.heading: What was the hare like?
bullets: He thought he had plenty of time: overconfident
teach.note: Reread the fable and underline clues about the hare. Model a full answer: 'I think the hare was proud because he said he could win with his eyes closed.' Ask pupils to find another.

teach.heading: What was the tortoise like?
bullets: He plodded on and never stopped: determined
teach.note: Contrast the tortoise's quiet reply with the hare's boast. Ask which character we should copy. Link to humility as a value we admire in Islam, without making false claims about texts.

teach.heading: Words in context
teach.note: Show how neighbouring words help with meaning: 'plodded on, step by step'. Ask pupils to replace each word with a simpler one and check it still makes sense.

teach.heading: Write an inference answer
bullets: Evidence: he lay down for a nap
Explain: he forgot the race was still going
teach.note: Model a P.E.E. style answer: Point, Evidence, Explain. Keep it simple for Year 3. Ask for sentence starters: 'This shows that...'

practice: How do you know the tortoise was determined?
Which word shows how the hare ran at the end?
What does plodded tell us about the tortoise?
independent: Write two sentences about the hare using 'I think... because...' with a quotation.
Write two sentences about the tortoise in the same way.
Choose a new adjective for each character and prove it with evidence.
exit: Complete: I think the hare was careless because...
What does boasted mean?
lessons.homework: Write a character description of the hare using three adjectives and evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and highlighted evidence. EAL: act the words boasted and plodded. Stretch: compare how the hare feels at the start and end.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Punctuating direct speech
objectives: Use inverted commas around spoken words
Punctuate speech with a comma, question mark or exclamation mark

keywords.def: the exact words someone says
speech marks that go around spoken words
words that say who is speaking, such as said Sara
marks such as full stops and commas

starter: Bismillah. What is a conjunction? Give one.
Add a prefix: __agree.
What is the hare's main feature?

teach.heading: Spoken words
bullets: Direct speech is what is actually said
Put inverted commas around the spoken words
"I could win any race," boasted the hare.
teach.note: Say a sentence aloud and ask the class to write exactly what you said. Introduce inverted commas as 'speech marks'. Pupils draw them in the air.

teach.heading: Where does the punctuation go?
teach.note: Show that the comma, question mark or exclamation mark goes inside the inverted commas. A capital letter starts the spoken words. Misconception: placing the comma outside the speech marks.

teach.heading: Reporting clause
teach.note: Collect better verbs than said. Compare: 'said the hare' and 'boasted the hare'. When the reporting clause comes first, a comma follows it and the spoken words begin with a capital letter.

teach.heading: New speaker, new line
bullets: Start a new line when someone else speaks
teach.note: Show a short conversation with new speakers on new lines. This helps the reader keep track of who is talking. Ask pupils to read it as a play.

teach.heading: Check your work
teach.note: Ask pupils to edit a sample with errors: "let us race said the tortoise." Correct together. Praise sharp checking.

practice: Add inverted commas: I am the fastest, said the hare.
Add punctuation: Where is the finish line asked the tortoise
Choose a better verb for said: boasted, shouted or whispered?
independent: Punctuate six sentences with speech.
Write a conversation of six lines between the fox and the hare. New speaker, new line.
Rewrite two sentences with the reporting clause at the start.
exit: Punctuate: Hurry up cried the hare.
Why does each new speaker need a new line?
lessons.homework: Write a short conversation between two animals in a fable, using correct punctuation.
lessons.send: SEND: use coloured speech bubble strips to separate spoken words. EAL: provide a bank of speech verbs. Stretch: split a spoken sentence around the reporting clause.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Planning our own fable
objectives: Choose characters, a flaw and a moral
Plan a fable in five parts

keywords.def: a weakness in a character, such as greed or pride
the trouble that happens in the story
how the problem is solved
a short outline of what will happen

starter: Bismillah. What is a moral?
Add inverted commas: Come with me said the fox.
Use the word because in a sentence.

teach.heading: What makes a good fable?
bullets: A problem caused by that flaw
A clear moral at the end
teach.note: Reread the main features from lesson 6. Ask pupils to name flaws: pride, greed, laziness, dishonesty. Explain that the moral should come from what happens, not just be added at the end.

teach.heading: Choose a moral first
teach.note: Link morals to values such as honesty and kindness. Select one together. Moral first means the whole plan works backwards from the lesson, which makes the ending meaningful.

teach.heading: A model plan
bullets: Characters: Sami the squirrel, Mrs Owl
Problem: he hides too many nuts
Moral: take only what you need
teach.note: Model: Sami the squirrel gathers far more nuts than he needs. Winter comes and he cannot carry the nuts home; other animals share and he learns to share too. Build the plan in five boxes: opening, build-up, problem, resolution, moral.

teach.heading: Five-part plan
bullets: Opening: meet the characters and setting
Build-up: the flaw begins to cause trouble
teach.note: Show an empty five-box grid. Pupils choose characters, setting, flaw and moral and write short notes in each box. Remind them to use notes, not full sentences.

teach.heading: Plan with detail
bullets: Choose two good adjectives for each character
Note a conjunction or adverb for each part
teach.note: Prompt pupils to think of language from Unit 1 for their plan: an expanded noun phrase for the setting and one line of dialogue.

practice: Match each flaw to a moral: pride, greed, dishonesty / honesty is best, take only what you need, be humble.
Name two animal characters and one adjective for each.
Where will your fable happen?
independent: Complete a five-part plan for your own fable.
Write one line of speech you will use.
Write two expanded noun phrases for your setting and main character.
exit: State your moral in one sentence.
Name your character's flaw.
lessons.homework: Tell your plan aloud to someone at home and note any improvements.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a ready-made plan with choices to circle. EAL: draw the plan before writing. Stretch: include a twist so the moral is not obvious at the start.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Writing the opening and build-up
objectives: Write an opening that introduces character and setting
Use time adverbs, conjunctions and noun phrases in the build-up

keywords.def: the start of a story that introduces characters and setting
where and when a story happens
the part where events lead to the problem
a word or phrase that adds information about when, where or how

starter: Bismillah. Say your moral aloud.
Write a noun phrase about a forest.
Add a time adverb: ___, the squirrel woke.

teach.heading: A strong opening
teach.note: Share a model opening: 'Once upon a time, in a thick green forest, lived a squirrel called Sami. Sami loved nuts so much that he never shared a single one.' Ask what we already know about Sami and what clues show his flaw.

teach.heading: Use Unit 1 skills
bullets: Expanded noun phrases: a tall oak tree with twisted roots
Time adverbs: One autumn morning, Soon, Later
teach.note: Highlight these features in the model. Ask pupils to find them in the model text. Emphasise 'show, not tell': let actions show the flaw.

teach.heading: Build-up
bullets: Show the flaw causing small problems
Use dialogue to show what characters think
teach.note: Model a build-up paragraph: 'Every day, Sami hurried through the forest, collecting more and more nuts. "I need them all," he muttered.' Discuss how the dialogue reveals the flaw.

teach.heading: Paragraphs
bullets: Start a new paragraph for a new time or place
teach.note: Explain that paragraphs help the reader. Pupils mark the paragraph breaks in the model. Check against their five-box plan.

teach.heading: Write and reread
bullets: Check capital letters and full stops
teach.note: Write alongside pupils for the first sentences, then let them write independently. Circulate to praise precise vocabulary and correct punctuation. Remind them to reread each sentence.

practice: Write the first sentence of your fable.
Add an expanded noun phrase to describe your setting.
Add a time adverb to start your build-up.
independent: Write the opening and build-up of your fable (about 8 sentences).
Include at least one line of direct speech.
Underline one expanded noun phrase and one conjunction.
exit: Which sentence in your writing shows the flaw?
Which time adverb did you use?
lessons.homework: Reread your writing aloud and fix any missing punctuation.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and a word bank; scribe if needed. EAL: allow first draft ideas in home language, then translate key vocabulary. Stretch: add a second line of speech and a simile.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Writing the problem, resolution and moral
objectives: Write the problem and resolution of a fable
End with a clear moral

keywords.def: the most exciting or serious part of a story
how the problem is solved
the lesson at the end
the final part of a story

starter: Bismillah. What does the build-up of a fable show?
Punctuate: Help cried the squirrel.
Use although in a sentence.

teach.heading: The problem
teach.note: Model the problem: 'One cold morning, the snow fell. Sami could not carry his nuts. He was stuck.' Explain how short sentences create tension and show the character's feelings.

teach.heading: The resolution
bullets: Another character helps or something changes
teach.note: Model: Mrs Owl and the other animals share their nuts with Sami; he gives away some of his. The change is shown through his actions, not just stated. Link to the value of sharing.

teach.heading: The moral
bullets: State the lesson in one sentence
Start with Moral: or The lesson is...
Make sure it matches the story
teach.note: Show different ways of ending: 'Moral: take only what you need.' Check that it matches the flaw. Ask pupils to give a reason why it matches.

teach.heading: Dialogue in the ending
bullets: Show how the character has changed
"Thank you," said Sami. "I will share from now on."
teach.note: Model a final line of speech. Pupils check punctuation. Point out the comma before the closing inverted commas.

teach.heading: Write the ending
teach.note: Pupils continue their stories. Remind them to check their plan and to keep sentences varied. Monitor for good verbs and punctuation.

practice: Write one short sentence to start the problem.
Write a line of speech for the resolution.
Write your moral.
independent: Write the problem, resolution and moral (about 8 sentences).
Include a line of dialogue with correct punctuation.
Check that your moral matches your character's flaw.
exit: Does your moral match your story? How do you know?
Underline one short sentence that builds tension.
lessons.homework: Read your whole fable aloud at home and mark one thing to improve.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frames for resolution and moral. EAL: read the model ending together first. Stretch: write a second paragraph with a surprise.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Editing, improving and publishing our fables
objectives: Proofread for punctuation, spelling and sense
Improve word choices and share your finished fable

keywords.def: check writing carefully for mistakes
make changes to improve writing
write or print a final neat copy to share
comments that help improve work

starter: Bismillah. Spell: disappear, misbehave, rewrite.
Punctuate: Come here called the owl.
Name three features of a fable.

teach.heading: Why edit?
bullets: Good writers always check their work
teach.note: Explain that editing is part of writing, not a punishment. Model on a sample paragraph with deliberate errors. Read it aloud to show how it helps us spot mistakes.

teach.heading: Checklist
bullets: Did I show my flaw and moral clearly?
teach.note: Display the checklist and ask pupils to tick items in their own book with a purple pen. Use the checklist on the sample text first.

teach.heading: Improve word choices
bullets: Replace said with a stronger verb
Replace nice with a precise adjective
teach.note: Show a flat sentence and improve it three ways: add an adjective, add a time adverb, replace the verb. Pupils improve at least three of their own sentences.

teach.heading: Peer feedback
teach.note: Pair pupils in the break-out rooms or on camera. Model kind, specific feedback such as 'I liked your simile because it helped me picture the owl'. Link to adab: kind and truthful speech.

teach.heading: Publish and celebrate
bullets: Read it aloud to the class
teach.note: Select volunteers to read. Praise effort and growth. End by recalling the morals created by the class and what they teach.

practice: Correct: "I am hungry said the fox."
Spell: unhappy, misspell, redo.
Replace said: "Go away!" said the hare.
independent: Edit your fable using the checklist and a purple pen.
Improve three sentences by changing verbs or adding adjectives.
Write a neat final copy of the first paragraph.
exit: Give your fable a title.
Write one thing you improved.
lessons.homework: Practise reading your fable aloud for sharing next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: use a simplified checklist with pictures. EAL: check one thing at a time. Stretch: write an alternative moral and rewrite the ending to match.
